issues.legal_issue: A tax law is not colourable legislation merely because it is intended to reduce compensation payable under an estate-acquisition scheme when its substance falls within the legislature’s taxing authority.
material_facts: The estate-acquisition law deducted agricultural income tax payable for the preceding year when calculating compensation.
The legislature increased agricultural income-tax rates, and the amended tax was actually payable when the acquisition law took effect.
The challengers alleged that the tax increase was intended to reduce their compensation, but the law in substance imposed agricultural income tax, a subject within the State Legislature’s authority.
issues.conclusion: The agricultural income-tax amendment was valid and was not colourable legislation; the alleged ulterior purpose did not invalidate a law within the legislature’s competence.
issues.legal_principle: The doctrine of colourable legislation concerns legislative competence, not the legislature’s motives or bona fides. A court examines the substance and true character of a law, including its effects and purpose as aids to that inquiry, to determine whether the legislature has transgressed its powers under cover of a different form. The principle that a legislature cannot do indirectly what it cannot do directly does not invalidate an indirect measure if the legislature could achieve the object directly. The Court distinguished State of Bihar v. Maharajah Kameshwar Singh, where provisions were outside the compensation head of power, and relied on the distinction between a genuine tax within List II, entry 46, and a purported compensation principle under List III, entry 42. It also referred to Attorney-General for Ontario v. Reciprocal Insurers, Attorney-General for Alberta v. Attorney-General for Canada, Union Colliery Co. of British Columbia Ltd. v. Bryden, Cunningham v. Tomeyhomma, Re Insurance Act of Canada, and Moran v. Deputy Commissioner for Taxation, New South Wales. Articles 31(2) and 31(4) govern the related acquisition and compensation challenge.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_tax_law: A party challenges the constitutionality of a law that imposes a tax.
predicates.legislature_has_authority_over_true_subj: The legislature that enacted the law has authority over the subject the law substantively regulates.
predicates.law_substantively_imposes_tax: The law actually imposes a tax, and the tax is an existing liability relevant to the compensation calculation.

issues.definition: When a tax law is challenged, the rule means that a legislature’s authority over the law’s true subject and the law’s substantive imposition of a tax lead to the tax law not being invalid as colourable legislation.

issues.legal_issue: Buildings within an estate that are used primarily to manage or administer it may vest in the State as part of an estate-abolition acquisition.
material_facts: The acquisition law provided for estate-management and office buildings within an estate to vest in the State.
The law provided compensation in respect of those buildings as part of the estate’s compensation calculation.
The acquisition law had been passed while pending legislation and received the President’s assent.
issues.conclusion: The legislature could provide for estate-management buildings to vest as appurtenances to the estate; the acquisition fell within Article 31(2) and received Article 31(4) protection when that clause’s conditions were met.
issues.legal_principle: A legislature may include buildings within an estate that are primarily used for its management or administration in an estate-abolition scheme, even if Indian law does not invariably treat buildings as part of the soil. Such acquisition falls within Article 31(2); if Article 31(4)’s conditions are satisfied, inadequacy of compensation does not defeat the acquisition. The relevant compensation legislative head is List III, entry 42.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_estate_acqui: A party challenges the constitutionality of a law acquiring an estate.
predicates.building_within_estate: The building lies within the estate being acquired.
predicates.building_used_primarily_for_estate_manag: The building is used primarily to manage or administer the estate.
predicates.acquisition_law_received_required_assent: The acquisition law met the applicable requirements for presidential assent to legislation pending when the Constitution commenced.

issues.definition: For a constitutional challenge to an estate acquisition, the rule means that a building within the estate used primarily for its management may validly vest when the acquisition law received the required assent.

issues.legal_issue: Acquisition of an estate owner’s private land in the possession of temporary tenants is not unconstitutional merely because compensation is calculated by reference to the produce rent payable by those tenants.
material_facts: The acquired private lands were in the possession of temporary tenants, who would hold them as tenants under the State after acquisition.
The acquisition covered the proprietor’s entire interest in those lands.
Compensation for the lands was assessed by reference to the income represented by the temporary tenants’ share of the produce payable to the proprietor.
The acquisition law received the President’s assent after being passed as a bill that had been pending when the Constitution commenced.
issues.conclusion: The acquisition provisions were not unconstitutional: the produce-rent measure did not show that compensation had been provided only for the proprietor’s interest and not for the entire interest acquired, and inadequacy of compensation could not be challenged under Article 31(4).
issues.legal_principle: Compensation for acquired property may be assessed on the basis of the property’s net income, and a rental or produce-rent measure is within the compensation legislative power in List III, entry 42. The Court followed Raja Suriya Pal Singh v. State of Uttar Pradesh. Where Article 31(4) applies, the adequacy of compensation is not open to challenge. The Court rejected the contention that the produce-rent measure compensated only the landlord’s interest, because the whole interest was acquired and the measure represented the property’s income.

rule.if: constitutional_challenge_to_estate_acquisition and private_land_occupied_by_temporary_tenants and entire_proprietary_interest_acquired and compensation_measured_by_property_income and acquisition_law_received_required_assent

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_estate_acqui: A party challenges the constitutionality of a law acquiring an estate.
predicates.private_land_occupied_by_temporary_tenan: The acquired private land is occupied by temporary tenants.
predicates.entire_proprietary_interest_acquired: The acquisition takes the proprietor’s entire interest in the land.
predicates.compensation_measured_by_property_income: Compensation is calculated by reference to income the property produces for its owner.
predicates.acquisition_law_received_required_assent: The acquisition law met the applicable requirements for presidential assent to legislation pending when the Constitution commenced.

issues.definition: For a constitutional challenge to an estate acquisition, the rule means that acquiring tenant-occupied private land is valid when the entire proprietary interest is acquired, compensation is measured by the land’s income, and the law received the required assent.

issues.legal_issue: A bill pending when the Constitution commenced may receive the protection applicable to such legislation even if the legislature amends it before passage.
material_facts: The estate-acquisition bill was pending before the State Legislature when the Constitution commenced.
The provision concerning private lands occupied by temporary tenants was added by amendment after the Constitution commenced.
The bill, as amended, was passed by the Legislature, reserved for the President’s consideration, and received the President’s assent.
issues.conclusion: The expression “passed by such Legislature” includes a bill passed with amendments, so the added provision was not excluded from Article 31(4)’s protection.
issues.legal_principle: Article 31(4) applies where a bill pending at the commencement of the Constitution is passed by the State Legislature and receives the President’s assent. “Passed by such Legislature” means passed with or without amendments, in accordance with the ordinary legislative procedure contemplated by Article 107. Thus, an amendment made after the Constitution commenced does not, by itself, remove the resulting law from Article 31(4)’s protection.

rule.if: constitutional_challenge_to_acquisition_law and bill_pending_when_constitution_commenced and legislature_passed_bill_with_amendments and bill_reserved_and_received_assent

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_acquisition_: A party challenges an acquisition law on the basis that it does not receive the protection available to certain pending bills.
predicates.bill_pending_when_constitution_commenced: The bill that became the challenged law was pending before the State Legislature when the Constitution commenced.
predicates.legislature_passed_bill_with_amendments: The State Legislature passed the bill after making one or more amendments.
predicates.bill_reserved_and_received_assent: The bill was reserved for the President’s consideration and received the President’s assent.

issues.definition: The rule means that an amended acquisition law receives pending-bill protection when its bill was pending at the Constitution’s commencement, was passed with amendments, and was reserved and assented to.

issues.legal_issue: A provision requiring compensation for acquired property to be paid in instalments is within the legislature’s power to prescribe the form and manner of compensation and is not colourable legislation merely because payment is deferred.
material_facts: The acquisition law required compensation, with interest, to be paid in annual instalments.
The law allowed the State to make full payment earlier.
The challengers argued that the instalment provision was colourable legislation.
issues.conclusion: The instalment provision was valid; it prescribed the form and manner of giving compensation and was not colourable legislation.
issues.legal_principle: List III, entry 42 includes legislative authority to prescribe the principles for determining compensation and the form and manner in which it is given. A provision governing the payment of compensation in instalments is within that subject and is not legislation about a non-existent or factually unrelated matter. The Court distinguished the provisions invalidated in State of Bihar v. Maharajah Kameshwar Singh.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_compensation: A party challenges the constitutionality of a provision governing how compensation for acquired property is paid.
predicates.law_prescribes_how_compensation_is_paid: The law specifies a method or schedule for paying compensation.

issues.definition: For a constitutional challenge to a compensation payment method, the rule means that a law prescribing how compensation is paid is valid.
